name: Peak of Inflated Expectations
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Why Success Stories Multiply Faster Than Successes
lesson.summary: The Peak of Inflated Expectations is the loudest phase of any hype cycle, when success stories, funding, and press coverage grow far faster than the technology's actual proven capability.
lesson.body:
The Peak of Inflated Expectations is the second and loudest stage of the hype cycle: media saturation, large funding rounds, and public expectations that exceed anything the current version of the technology can actually support. Loudness at this stage correlates poorly with the technology's real maturity, which is exactly what makes it dangerous to navigate.

The mechanism is straightforward once named. A small number of genuine early wins, a proof of concept demonstration, a pilot project, a viral demo, get amplified through press coverage, conference keynotes, analyst reports, and venture pitches. Because attention and capital are cheap relative to the engineering effort required to actually solve a hard problem, the number of people talking about a technology grows far faster than the number who have gotten it to reliably work.

The dot-com era of the late 1990s is a clear, well documented example. Internet retail startups were valued and discussed as though they had already solved logistics, customer acquisition cost, and margin problems that in most cases they had not solved at all. Investors and journalists pointed to early user growth curves and simply drew a straight line upward, treating the first eighteen months of a company's life as a reliable preview of its next twenty years. Expectations were extrapolated linearly from growth rates that could not realistically hold at that pace once a company moved past its earliest, most enthusiastic adopters, and headlines treated the extrapolation as though it were already settled fact rather than one optimistic scenario among several.

Two dynamics make the peak especially treacherous. The first is reflexivity: rising expectations attract more capital, which funds more visible activity, which raises expectations further, a loop that can run for a while with only a loose connection to underlying capability. The second is selection bias in reporting: journalists and conference organizers need dramatic stories, and it is about to change everything is simply a more compelling headline than it mostly does not work yet, so the coverage itself skews optimistic independent of the facts.

Recall Technology Adoption Curves: the Peak of Inflated Expectations arrives early in real adoption terms, typically while actual usage is still concentrated among innovators and early adopters, plus speculators who never intended to be genuine users at all. That means the noise to signal ratio about real capability is at its worst exactly when public attention, and often public investment, is at its highest.

What goes up during a peak driven mostly by a reflexive attention and funding loop, rather than by delivered value, has nowhere to go but down once the first wave of pilots reports back with underwhelming results. That correction is what sets up the next stage, the Trough of Disillusionment, and understanding the peak's mechanics is what makes the trough legible as a predictable consequence rather than a mysterious reversal.
